The Arctic hookear sculpin Artediellus uncinatus, a small-bodied cottid inhabiting cold waters of the North Atlantic and Arctic oceans, reaches a maximum recorded total length of 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters] in adulthood. This modest size is typical of the genus and is accompanied by a correspondingly low body mass; field studies indicate that the asymptotic wet weight of adult individuals is approximately 10.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 10.5 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions applied to local populations. The species maintains a benthic lifestyle on soft substrates, where it preys primarily on small crustaceans and polychaetes. Growth rates appear to be relatively slow, consistent with the low metabolic demands imposed by the persistently cold thermal regime of its environment. Mature females are readily distinguishable from males during the spawning season by their distended abdomens, though sexual dimorphism in overall size is minimal. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that these size parameters are largely conserved within Artediellus, reflecting a common evolutionary response to similar ecological constraints across high-latitude continental shelves.

Reproductive development in female Arctic hookear sculpin proceeds at a notably small body size, with puberty occurring at a total length of 4 centimeters [Lp = 4 centimeters]. At this stage, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 0.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.6 grams], indicating that females become reproductively mature well before achieving their ultimate body dimensions. This pattern of early maturation relative to asymptotic size is often interpreted as an adaptation to low adult survival probabilities or unpredictable recruitment environments in polar ecosystems. The onset of gonadal activity is accompanied by vitellogenesis, and gravid females can be observed carrying demersal, adhesive eggs that are deposited in sheltered microhabitats on the seafloor. The relatively small size at maturity suggests that energy allocation shifts from somatic growth to reproductive investment at an early stage of the life cycle, a strategy common among small-bodied, iteroparous marine fishes inhabiting food-limited environments. Field surveys have confirmed that individuals as small as 4 centimeters [Lp = 4 centimeters] consistently possess fully developed ovaries.

At the time of hatching, yolk-sac larvae of Artediellus uncinatus emerge from their chorions at a remarkably small wet weight at birth of 0.006 grams [Wwb = 0.006 grams]. This minuscule neonatal mass reflects the limited yolk reserves packaged within eggs that typically measure around 2.25 mm in diameter, based on data from the closely related Artediellus atlanticus. The larvae are initially non-feeding and rely entirely on endogenous yolk absorption during the first days post-eclosion, a period during which they remain in close association with the benthos. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs shortly after mouth opening and yolk-sac resorption, at which point the tiny free-swimming larvae must locate suitable prey items, primarily copepod nauplii. Mortality during this early life stage is presumably high, as is typical for fish species that produce large numbers of small offspring. The low birth mass imposes strong constraints on larval foraging ability and vulnerability to starvation, underscoring the critical importance of temporal match between hatch timing and peak planktonic productivity in Arctic waters.

Under the persistent thermal conditions typical of this species' habitat, specifically a water temperature of 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C], the maximum reproduction rate of Artediellus uncinatus has been estimated from fecundity data. Observations of gravid females from related populations indicate that each female produces approximately 62 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 62 eggs per spawning event], and coupling this with an annual spawning frequency yields roughly 22 offspring per female per year [Ri = roughly 22 offspring per female per year]. The estimated maximum lifespan in the wild attains 3650 days [am = 3650 days] at the same ambient temperature of 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C]. This extended longevity is notable for a fish of such modest size and is consistent with the extremely slow metabolic rates and delayed senescence observed in many polar ectotherms. The combination of low temperature, reduced metabolic demand, and low predation pressure in deep-water Arctic habitats likely contributes to this exceptional lifespan. Longevity records from tagging studies of Artediellus atlanticus support these values, suggesting that a decadal lifespan is plausible for the genus.

The Arctic hookear sculpin's life history reflects a slow-paced strategy where adult females, reaching an asymptotic mass of 10.5 grams [Wwi = 10.5 grams] and a total length of 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters], regularly live up to 10 years [am = up to 10 years] in the cold Arctic at a temperature of 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C]waters. This extended longevity under a thermal regime averaging 2.4 °C [T = 2.4 °C] stands in contrast to short-lived temperate cottids, which rarely survive beyond three or four years. The persistence of these fish in high-latitude environments likely reflects a trade-off between slow growth and extended reproductive windows, allowing iteroparous females to spread reproductive effort across many seasons. This bet-hedging strategy buffers populations against the stochastic recruitment success characteristic of polar marine ecosystems. The small size at birth and early puberty further reinforce an overall life-history syndrome shaped by cold, resource-limited conditions, with each trait contributing to the species' ecological resilience in a changing Arctic.
